Text.Text: Every time you walk in I hear the crowd that should be here. You closed the backroom bill, you took the final bloom for yourself, and I retired the poster. Nothing left down there I'd charge admission for. Go be somebody's main event.

A new challenger approaches the -- no. Can't sell it. The walk is right, but the hands are half a beat apart. You're good, friend, and good gets buried down there. When the paired blades have nothing left to learn the ordinary way, come back. I'll write you a headline worth the ink.

A new name steps onto the card, ladies and gentles, a stylist of the paired blade like the circuit has never -- and that's my whole audience tonight: you and a mop bucket. Habit. Quiet version, then. Somebody's running a second bill in the backrooms under this club, selling my Tempest Bloom as blood sport. Their opening act is six adepts throwing a bootleg of the form. I've cut you a key to the sealed door behind the main pit. Go down, retire all six, and lift their Backroom Bout Ledger on the way out. I want to know every fight they've booked.

There's the spine I was going to invent for your introduction. The key fits the sealed door behind the main pit. Six adepts, one coded ledger. Don't read it on the way up -- some of those bookings will put you off your dinner.

The only act I ever announced twice in one breath. Both blades open outward like petals -- pretty, the crowd sighs -- then the whole shape collapses inward and it's a storm with edges. Done right, it's the finish nobody sees and everybody remembers. Done the way they teach it downstairs, it's butchery with choreography.

Promoters who got greedy and fighters who got tired of my rules. They sealed off the old backrooms -- the door behind the main pit, the one your key fits. Past it, the halls are theirs: pit after pit, no bell, no doctor, no me. Everything you need to hurt is inside.

Undercard material, but don't smile yet. Six of them, and they train on people who can't leave. Any one alone would make a decent show against you. They won't come alone -- that's not the kind of bill it is. Warm up before you go down. I mean that.
You're still on the undercard, friend. Six adepts under the club, and their Backroom Bout Ledger comes up with you. The door behind the main pit still answers to your key.
You came up walking and the noise downstairs stopped. That's the review I wanted. The ledger -- let's see who they've been booking to bleed.

Ha. Half these names are fighters I banned for exactly this. You just cancelled six acts and the crowd upstairs doesn't even know it owes you. Take the purse. When you've caught your breath, come back -- the bill goes deeper than its undercard.

On to the main card, ladies and -- still just you. Good. Your ledger names five specialists: their word for fighters who've drilled the bloom until it almost works. They keep their pits live through a ring shock regulator they've rewired to punish anyone who fights fair. Go back down, put all five out of the business, and rip that Ring Shock Regulator off the wall. I want their stage lights out.

Announce yourself however you like down there -- they already know your name from what you did to their undercard. Five specialists, one rewired regulator. Bring it back with the wiring intact. I want to show it to some people who called me paranoid.

Faster than the adepts and twice as vain. Each one has polished a single petal of the bloom to a mirror shine -- one leads left, one only counters, one throws both blades wide and gambles you'll flinch. Alone, each is a solvable puzzle. In those pits they'll rotate on you like a rehearsed finale. Solve fast.

A ring shock regulator keeps an honest pit honest -- kills the current the instant a fighter goes down. They rewired theirs to do the opposite. Fighter drops, the floor bites them back up. That's how they've been selling half-dead men as comeback stories. Pull it off the wall and the pits go back to being merely lethal.

Because I sold spectacle and somebody else sold blood, and blood outdraws me ten to one on this moon. Promoters moved downstairs, my old sound rig went with them, and half a season later there's a second club under my club. I book the crowd. They book the graves. That ends bout by bout, starting with yours.
Five specialists still standing between you and my good opinion of this week. The Ring Shock Regulator comes off the wall after they come off the card.
You smell like ozone and somebody else's blood. Beautiful. The regulator -- hand it here.

Look at this butchery -- they bridged the safety cutout with a credit chit. A credit chit. Somebody's whole life ended over five decicreds of copper. You've turned their main card into an empty room, friend. Next time you come in, we talk about the man guarding the deep door -- and that talk happens before you go anywhere near him.

Here's where I stop selling and start warning. Past the pits there's a gate to the deep rooms, and the gate has a name: the warden. Old pit champion, never lost, retired into the job of ending anyone who knocks. He wears a pit sigil cracked down the middle from the night he killed his own trainer in what the ledger politely calls an exhibition. Take him down and bring me that Cracked Pit Sigil. And hear me clearly -- nobody headlines against the warden alone. The crowd used to love a trio against him because a trio occasionally lived. Book two fighters worth their purse before you knock.

Company. Say it back to me. -- Good. The deep gate is past the last live pit; he'll open it himself when you knock, because ceremony is the one habit he kept. When it's done, bring the cracked sigil straight up. Don't stop to read the walls down there.

Fourteen seasons, no losses, and I called every one of his fights from the good microphone. He does the bloom the way a glacier does patience -- slow openings you don't notice until both his edges are already through your guard. When the backroom bill started, they gave him the deep door because nobody would buy a ticket to him anymore. Fear is bad box office.

Because I've read his whole record and I wrote half of it. One fighter gives the warden exactly what his style eats: a single rhythm to learn. Three rhythms, and he has to choose -- choosing is the only thing he's slow at. Every corpse the deep door has taken went down there proud and alone. Be less proud. Live longer.

Every backroom fighter carries a pit sigil -- their license, their name, their tally. His cracked the night his trainer died on his blades, and he kept wearing it broken, which tells you what kind of sermon he is. On my desk, that sigil closes fourteen seasons of business the bill has been trading on. It's the difference between hurting them and unlicensing them.
The warden's gate is still shut and I haven't heard the kind of quiet that means he's gone. Two blades beside you, then knock. The Cracked Pit Sigil comes back with the news.
The whole club felt that. Lights flickered mid-bout upstairs and I knew. Show me the sigil.

Cracked twice now. Fitting. You just did what fourteen seasons of contenders couldn't, and you did it smart -- I counted three sets of footsteps on my stairs. That's not weakness, that's stagecraft. Rest. What's left behind that gate is the promoter's inner circle, and they will not queue up politely.

Behind the warden's gate you'll find the reason the bill exists: the inner circle. Four of them -- the promoter's own fighters, paid in what the ledger calls appearance fees and I call bounties. They're the ones who taught a torture-pit full of amateurs my Tempest Bloom. Retire all four, and on the last one you'll find the Promoter's Payout Chit -- the money trail with the promoter's own thumb on it. That chit buys us the master's door. Nothing else will.

That's the confidence I used to script for headliners, except you've earned the material. Four fighters, one signed chit. If the twins are the last two standing, do not let them set the tempo. Come back rich in evidence.

My best students, once. I taught them the bloom for the crowd; the promoter re-taught it for the payout. One announces her strikes the way I announce fighters -- listen and you'll live. One only fights out of corners. The twins finish each other's combinations, so never stand between them. I'd say take them one at a time, but they won't offer, and past the warden's gate nobody comes running when you shout. Keep your company close.

Backroom purses never touch anything with a name attached -- except one thing. The promoter signs payout chits by hand, because he trusts banks even less than fighters. Whoever holds the circle's chit holds proof of every death he's paid for. It also opens his last door. He built the master's room to admit money and nothing else, which tells you the order he values things in.

Not yet. Ask me when the circle's done and I'll tell you about the only act I ever refused to announce twice. Short version to hold you over: the master's final bloom emptied this house once -- fighters, bookies, the boy who sold caf at the door. I sold the tickets to it. That's my share of the bill, and it's why I'm still at this desk instead of retired somewhere with weather.
The inner circle is still drawing appearance fees. Four retirements, then the Promoter's Payout Chit off the last one standing. The master's door stays shut without it.
Four empty dressing rooms downstairs. You're a wrecking crew with footwork, friend. The chit -- careful. The ink is blood in more ways than one.

His thumbprint, his hand, his numbers. Twenty years I wanted this, and now I mostly feel tired. That's the whole bill cancelled except the headliner -- and before you square your shoulders at me, sit down for the next part. When you're ready to hear about the master, I'll be here. Not selling anything, for once.

No introductions this time. The master was my headliner the year this club mattered -- the Tempest Bloom isn't something he learned, it's something he finishes. In the final act of his last main event, the bloom opened wider than anything I'd ever announced, and when it closed, the house was empty. Everyone the storm could reach, it took. He's been in the deepest room since, running the bill so people keep coming to him. The chit opened his door. Beyond it, hear this like a contract: nobody survives his final bloom alone. Nobody ever has. Walk in with two beside you or don't walk in. Beat him, and the bloom stops being his.

Then that's the card -- you and two names I'll never get to announce, against the last act on the bill. I'd wish you luck, but I've watched you work; luck is for the undercard. Bring me the only proof that counts. Walk back up those stairs.

He wields the thing you came here to earn, at its full height, with fifteen years of corpses for sparring notes. So no -- not at his own form, not the way he does it. Beat him at yours. His bloom needs room and rhythm, and three fighters who refuse him both are the one bill he's never fought. Take his tempo, take his space, and the storm is just a man with two swords and a long memory.

Then it's yours. That's not a figure of speech -- the form passes to whoever finishes its keeper, and that custom is older than my club and older than this moon's bad plumbing. You'd walk up those stairs carrying the real Tempest Bloom, the one I used to sell as a miracle at two credits a seat. Be gentler with it than he was. Or at least pick better audiences.

Because I called the fight that emptied this house, and the count that night was one hero at a time, in a queue, being brave. The bloom devours single rhythms -- that is what it is for. Two beside you isn't a crutch, it's the counter-form. Even the crowd knew it back then. They only ever bet on trios against him, and the crowd is a fool about everything except dying.
The deepest door is open and the headliner is still breathing. I keep the lights on up here until you finish the bill. Two beside you. Don't make me announce a memorial.
The floor stopped humming an hour ago. Fifteen years I've felt his footwork through these boards, and now the building is just a building. Say it, so I can stop holding my breath.

Then the bill is closed and the house is yours. No purse covers this, but take it anyway -- and take the thing he can't hold anymore. That storm with edges is your act now, friend. Somewhere, every time you use it, a washed-up announcer is doing your introduction to an empty room, and it is a beautiful introduction. Now get out of my club and go be worth it.
Back to the job.
Put my name on the card.
What exactly is the Tempest Bloom?
Who's running this second bill?
What are these adepts like?
Not tonight, Brask.
Here. Every bout they ever booked.
Run the card by me again.
Five specialists. Done.
How do their specialists fight?
What does this regulator do?
How did the bill get this deep under your club?
I'll pass for now.
One regulator, wiring intact.
Back to the warden.
Then I'll knock. With company.
Who was the warden before the door?
Why bring others? I've done fine alone.
What does the sigil matter?
Not until I've picked my seconds.
The warden's sigil. It's over.
Back to the circle.
Four names. Consider them cancelled.
Who are the four?
What's on this payout chit?
And after them -- the master?
Give me a day first.
The promoter's chit. Signed and everything.
Tell me about the main event again.
Then it's the main event. All three of us.
Can he be beaten at his own form?
What happens to the bloom when he's gone?
Why do you keep saying two beside me?
Not tonight. This one deserves my best.
The final bloom is finished. He's gone.
